en.content:
The Tai Po blaze inquiry has become more than a tragedy recounting itself—it is a test of how Hong Kong’s public-safety systems learn, adapt, and protect residents. Reports that there are no standard operating protocols for dealing with failed fire alarms, coupled with testimony that key records may be missing, point to a risk that procedures can drift without clear accountability. In a well-run city, emergency response is not just about bravery at the scene; it is also about repeatable standards that reduce uncertainty when every second counts.

At the same time, it would be misleading to treat this as simple incompetence. Fires involve complex variables: alarm malfunctions, building design constraints, communication breakdowns, and human judgement under stress. The proper question for the inquiry is therefore not who to blame first, but what to fix so that the next incident does not hinge on gaps in documentation or the absence of clear guidance. If standard protocols are lacking for non-functioning alarms, then the remedy should be framed around system design—clear thresholds for escalation, documented checks, and communication protocols across agencies—rather than relying on ad hoc decisions.

Hong Kong’s public expects more than investigations that end with condolences. While the government and relevant departments should be allowed to conduct their assessments in a lawful and orderly manner, the community also has a legitimate interest in transparent findings and follow-through. Independent scrutiny is valuable precisely because it can surface weaknesses that routine internal reviews might overlook, especially in the “grey zone” between technology failure and operational response. That includes improving record-keeping and ensuring that deployment and access logs are complete and auditable.

Finally, this case resonates beyond one estate or one incident. Effective safety management is part of the city’s broader social contract: residents should feel that lessons are institutionalised, not merely remembered. As the inquiry continues, the most constructive outcome would be measurable changes—updated procedures, revised training, better alarm-failure contingencies, and strengthened documentation—so that public trust is rebuilt on concrete improvements rather than on explanations alone.

zh.content:
今次大埔爆炸火災調查最值得社會警惕、亦最反映制度盲點嘅，係「保障唔落地」。有關部門指未有就「失效警報」作出標準操作程序，亦有證供指未能記錄有消防員進入涉事大廈。呢兩點加埋一齊，就唔係單純事故「唔好彩」，而係顯示應變流程、資訊留存、指揮鏈條等關鍵環節，可能存在制度性缺口。當火災發生時，時間同程序係生命線；如果「事前無標準、事中靠經驗」、甚至「事後無可核對嘅紀錄」，就會令問責困難、令風險無法被重複預防。

更令人不安嘅係，公眾真正關心嘅並唔止係「做咗咩」，而係「點解唔做應該做嘅」。獨立調查如果只停留喺宣稱某些措施「已經有」或「按當時情況」，而唔深入拆解每一個流程位（警報失靈時有冇明確判斷門檻？派員、入屋、通訊、回報同交接各自責任係咩？紀錄系統有冇硬性留痕？），就難以回應市民對安全制度有效性的焦慮。安全唔係靠運氣，唔係靠個別人「醒目」；安全要係可被驗證、可被訓練、可被檢討嘅系統工程。

因此，我哋嘅立場應該係：要追究責任，但更要推動「制度修補」而唔係「口頭承諾」。當失效警報成為現實場景，應有一套清晰SOP處理策略，包括備援偵測方式、升級通報機制、消防人員進出與位置留存、以及事後可追溯嘅數據化紀錄。與此同時，獨立委員會嘅角色必須延伸至提出具體改革建議，例如要求以可量化指標衡量訓練成效、定期演練涵蓋警報失靈情境、並確立錯漏時嘅責任分層。只要呢啲「可操作」嘅改動唔落實，任何「已改善」都會變成空話。

再講得直接啲：在高密度居住環境下，消防係全城共同承擔嘅公共安全。大埔火災調查唔應只係一場審訊，更應係一個迫使制度升級嘅轉捩點。市民需要嘅唔係只為平息輿論嘅說法，而係確保下一次警報失靈、煙未散、樓未穩嘅時候，系統仍能自動穩住節奏、減少盲點，讓救援由「事後補救」變成「事前防線」。

en.topic_summary:
A mainland Chinese woman has been acquitted of fraud over allegedly using a fake academic degree to obtain Hong Kong’s Top Talent visa, after a magistrate accepted the possibility that her agent made the false application.



Shatin Magistrates’ Courts. Photo: Kelly Ho/HKFP. 



Magistrate Raymond Wong found Xu Lina, 36, not guilty of conspiracy to defraud at the Shatin Magistrates’ Courts on Monday, according to local media.
